quote: Suche zu beweisen, dass die Umkehrung einer stetigen, nicht differenzirbaren Funktion stets unendlich vieldeutig ist.
english: Try to prove that the inverse of a continuous, non-differentiable function is always infinitely many-valued.
topic: The page records a task to prove that the inverse of a continuous nowhere-differentiable function is infinitely many-valued, a plan for a non-Gaussian probability theory modelled on non-Euclidean geometry, and a sketch showing that when the resultant of n forms is nonzero the variables are integral algebraic functions of the forms.

triage.modern_statement: Let f be a continuous real function on an interval that is nowhere differentiable. Show that f has no single-valued inverse on any subinterval, meaning its fibres f^{-1}(y) = {x : f(x) = y} are infinite. Read literally ('always infinitely many-valued'), this says every level set in the range of f is infinite. A weaker reading says this holds for many values y: a dense, residual (comeagre) or full-measure set of them. The standard route is through monotonicity. A function that is monotone on an interval is differentiable almost everywhere there, so a nowhere-differentiable function can be monotone on no interval (it is 'nowhere monotone'). The question then becomes how large the level sets of a continuous nowhere-monotone function are.
triage.answered_by: Two results settle this. The first is Lebesgue's theorem (1904): monotone functions are differentiable almost everywhere. So a continuous nowhere-differentiable function is monotone on no interval, and its inverse branches over any interval are never single-valued. The second is K. M. Garg, 'On level sets of a continuous nowhere monotone function', Fundamenta Mathematicae 52 (1963), 59–68, Theorem 1. For any continuous function that is monotone on no interval, the level set f^{-1}(y) is perfect, and therefore uncountable (much more than infinite), for a residual set of values y in the range. The literal claim for every y is false. Garg's result is generic, not universal, and later work by P. Allaart on the Takagi–van der Waerden functions (2013–14) found nowhere-differentiable functions whose level sets are finite for almost every y.

evidence.claim: Lebesgue proved, in a theorem published in 1904, that a monotone function must be differentiable almost everywhere. So a nowhere-differentiable continuous function cannot be monotone on any interval.
Garg, 'On level sets of a continuous nowhere monotone function', Fundamenta Mathematicae 52 (1963), 59–68.

Garg's Theorem 1 says that for any continuous function f which is monotone on no interval, the level set at level y is perfect, and hence uncountable, for a set of y-values residual in the range of f. Because the Takagi function is nowhere differentiable, it is monotone on no interval, so the theorem applies to it.

For the Takagi–van der Waerden functions f_r, which are continuous and nowhere differentiable: for every r ≥ 2 the level set L_r(y) is finite for almost every y, while L_r(f_r(x)) is uncountable for almost every x. So 'infinitely many-valued for every value' fails in the measure sense.

triage.why: This is a genuine research question in real analysis about the structure of the fibres (level sets) of nowhere-differentiable functions. It is not among Hilbert's 23 problems or the 24th problem, and I found no source that links this diary entry to any later work. The question was answered in substance by Lebesgue's 1904 theorem, which rules out monotone pieces and hence single-valued inverses, together with Garg's 1963 theorem, which gives uncountable perfect level sets for a residual set of values. The strong literal version ('always', for every value) is false, as the almost-everywhere finite level sets of the Takagi-type functions show. Research continues on level sets of specific nowhere-differentiable functions such as the Takagi and van der Waerden functions (Allaart; Lagarias–Maddock), so the area is still active. Confidence is medium for two reasons: the diary wording is ambiguous between the generic and universal readings, and I could not confirm that the source for the 1904 date is peer-reviewed.
